name: Microsoft SwiftKey
platforms: iOS (discontinued 5 October 2022, later relisted; theming detail below is from the documented era)
evidence_basis: Microsoft's own SwiftKey support documentation (the best first-party theming docs of the three closed-source keyboards researched), plus community reverse-engineering tooling that documents the on-disk theme format: rwiftkey-themes (VegaBobo), XSwiftkey / SwiftkeyXthemes (nijel8, Xposed), and the long-running XDA SwiftKey theming scene. SwiftKey is the most useful of the three closed-source references because the package format is partially known, not merely inferred.
rendering_approach: Hybrid, with a clearer split than Gboard between the two theme families. FAMILY A - built-in / store themes: predominantly per-key drawing. Community teardowns of the APK note that built-in themes under assets/themes 'use more XML and less PNG', i.e. keys are drawn from declarative XML state drawables and shape definitions with raster 9-patches used where a key cap needs a bitmap look; each key has its own background drawable with normal/pressed states. FAMILY B - Photo Themes (the feature this research is about): whole-image background paste behind a per-key overlay layer, exactly the Gboard model. Microsoft's own wording is the giveaway - the brightness slider 'determines how much of the photo is visible behind the keys', which only makes sense if the photo is a single layer behind semi-transparent keys. Crucially SwiftKey exposes MORE control over that overlay than Gboard does, and differently per platform: on Android you get a 'key borders' on/off toggle and, separately, a 'symbols on keys' on/off toggle (i.e. you can suppress the secondary symbol glyphs entirely so the photo reads more cleanly); on iOS you instead get a 'key background' choice of 'shades of grey or transparent' plus a separate key pop-up color picker. The iOS 'shades of grey or transparent' control is effectively a per-key scrim, sitting on top of the global photo scrim - a two-level dimming model worth noting. [uncertain - the XML-heavy vs PNG split for built-in themes comes from XDA community teardowns rather than Microsoft documentation, and the internal drawable/state mechanics are not published]
selector_and_state_model: No public author-facing selector syntax; SwiftKey has never shipped a theme SDK or documented schema. What the on-disk format and the UI together imply: theming is a fixed slot map, addressed by a combination of KEY ROLE and STATE encoded into resource FILE NAMES rather than by a rule language. The concrete evidence is the naming convention of theme drawables surfaced by the XDA scene - e.g. 'key_extended_normal.9.png', which decomposes as <role: key_extended, i.e. the wider functional/extended keys> + <state: normal> + <9-patch>. That naming pattern (role + state + density folder) is the whole selector model: to target pressed state you ship the corresponding *_pressed asset; to target a different key class you ship the corresponding role prefix. Roles observable from the product: normal letter keys, extended/functional keys, spacebar, the enter/action key, shift, delete, and numeric/symbol keys. States observable: normal and pressed at minimum. Not exposed and not evidenced: per-key-code targeting, shift/caps-state-specific art, disabled state, or focus. Photo Themes bypass the slot map almost entirely - they are a parameterized template (photo + crop + brightness + border flag + symbols flag) rather than an authored asset set, which is why they cannot be exported or synced. [uncertain - the role/state taxonomy is reconstructed from a single documented filename example plus product behavior; the full slot list and exact naming rules are not published]
rendering_pipeline: Android: InputMethodService with a custom View hierarchy drawn via Canvas + Android Drawables (including 9-patch NinePatchDrawable and XML StateListDrawable/shape drawables loaded from the theme's resources folder), not Jetpack Compose. The theme system is essentially a runtime resource loader - SwiftKey resolves drawables from an unpacked theme directory in its own data dir rather than only from compiled APK resources, which is precisely what makes the community's file-swapping approach work at all. iOS (during the documented era): a keyboard app extension with UIKit custom views. Per-keystroke cost is the standard invalidate-the-touched-key-rect pattern; the notable documented performance hazard on iOS was not the theme layer but CoreText emoji glyph memory retention, which is a separate long-standing SwiftKey iOS issue. [uncertain - the specific view/drawable classes are inferred from the observable resource format and Android platform norms; Microsoft publishes no architecture detail]
compositing_scrim_model: The best-documented scrim of the three, with a real published default number. Stack, bottom to top: photo -> global brightness scrim -> optional per-key background/border layer -> key labels -> optional secondary symbol glyphs -> key pop-ups. The global scrim is exposed as a single 'brightness' slider whose semantics Microsoft states directly: it 'determines how much of the photo is visible behind the keys'. ANDROID DEFAULT: 45%. That 45% figure is the single most citable number in this whole research area - it is a shipped, documented, first-party default for 'how much to dim a user photo so keyboard labels stay legible', and it sits right at the boundary of the Gboard community's 'keep it under 40%' folk guidance. Treat ~40-50% as the industry-converged default scrim strength. IOS BEHAVIOR IS DIFFERENT AND MORE ADVANCED: Microsoft documents that on iOS SwiftKey 'will try and determine the optimum brightness for your photo', then lets the user override with the same slider. That is an automatic per-image scrim computation - almost certainly luminance analysis of the cropped region - and it is the closest thing any of the three closed-source keyboards has to automated legibility enforcement. iOS additionally layers a SECOND, per-key scrim via the 'key background: shades of grey or transparent' control. No blur is exposed on either platform, and the scrim color is not user-settable. [uncertain - that the iOS auto-brightness is luminance-based is an inference; Microsoft says only 'optimum brightness' without describing the method]
asset_types: Raster PNG including 9-patch PNG (documented example: 'key_extended_normal.9.png'), plus XML resources - built-in themes are described as using 'more XML and less PNG', with XML carrying colors, shapes and state lists and PNG carrying the bitmap key-cap art. DENSITY BUCKETING IS REAL AND EXPLICIT here, unlike Gboard's photo path: the XDA theming workflow instructs authors to place edited PNG and XML files into 'hdpi', 'ldpi', 'xhdpi' and 'mdpi' folders, i.e. the theme package carries the standard Android density ladder and SwiftKey picks the right bucket at load time. For Photo Themes specifically, the asset is a single user-supplied raster from the gallery, cropped and stored per-theme - no density variants, since it is scaled at runtime. No vector/SVG, Lottie, or video assets are evidenced anywhere in the format. [uncertain - the density folder list and the 9-patch filename come from community tutorials rather than Microsoft docs; the current format may have consolidated buckets]
theme_package_manifest_format: The most concretely documented package format of the three items, thanks to the rwiftkey-themes project. STRUCTURE of a distributable community theme package: a zip archive (optionally renamed to the '.rwift' extension purely for convenience of sharing via Telegram/file manager) containing exactly two top-level members - (1) a directory named with a random UUID holding all theme resources, and (2) a JSON manifest file. The manifest is named 'themelist.json' in its canonical form; for custom/community packs the rwiftkey workflow requires renaming it to 'themelist_custom.json' so SwiftKey merges it with rather than replaces the built-in list. TWO NAMES ARE HARDCODED IN SWIFTKEY'S OWN CODE and cannot be changed: the manifest must be called 'themelist.json' and its parent folder must be called 'themes'. VERSIONING is carried in three places that must agree - the theme folder name, the resources folder name, and the themelist.json content all embed version numbers, and community authors must bump all three in lockstep for a theme to load on a given SwiftKey build. INSIDE the UUID folder: a 'resources' folder holding the density-bucketed PNG/9-patch/XML assets described above. BUILT-IN themes live at assets/themes inside the APK using the same layout. STORE-DOWNLOADED themes are written as ZIP files to /sdcard/Android/data/com.touchtype.swiftkey/themes. ROOT-INSTALLED themes are placed into SwiftKey's private data directory under /data/data/com.touchtype.swiftkey (this is why rwiftkey requires root - 'SwiftKey stores user themes on its own data folder, so we need root access to move theme to this folder'). LEGACY ERA: SwiftKey previously distributed themes as separate signed theme APKs, and SwiftKey verified the APK was signed with Microsoft/SwiftKey keys, so unofficial theme APKs would not load - a hard blocker the community only routed around via Xposed hooks or root file placement. Note what the manifest schema does NOT have publicly: the actual field names and types inside themelist.json have never been published, only its filename, its role as a theme index, and the fact that it carries version numbers. [uncertain - themelist.json's internal field list, types, and whether it holds style tokens or only an index of theme entries, is genuinely unknown; the structural facts (uuid folder, hardcoded names, three-place versioning, disk paths, root requirement) are well-attested by rwiftkey and XSwiftkey documentation]
token_count_tiering: A clear two-tier system, and the tiers are unusually cleanly separated. SIMPLE TIER (Photo Themes) - Android exposes exactly 4 user-settable properties: photo choice, crop/position (pinch-to-zoom + drag; rotation NOT supported on Android), brightness (default 45%), key borders on/off, and symbols-on-keys on/off (that is 5 counting crop as a property). iOS exposes a different 5: photo choice, crop/position/rotation (rotation IS supported on iOS), brightness (auto-computed, user-overridable), key pop-up color, and key background (grey shades or transparent). ADVANCED TIER (authored themes) - no published token count, but the asset-slot model implies dozens of addressable slots: every role x state x density combination in the resources folder is effectively a token, plus the XML color/shape definitions. A reasonable read is 'tens of slots, addressed by filename convention rather than by a named-token vocabulary', which is a materially different design from a JSON token map. Design lesson: SwiftKey proves you can ship a 4-5 control consumer tier over a much larger internal slot map without ever exposing the slot map to end users. [uncertain - no official number exists for the advanced tier; the count is inferred from the resource-directory structure]
theme_versioning_forward_compat: Versioning exists and is explicit but brittle - it is build-coupled rather than schema-coupled. Version numbers are embedded in three places (theme folder name, resources folder name, themelist.json) and community authors report having to change all three to make a theme work on a given SwiftKey version; the community guidance is literally that themes can be made to work 'on any SwiftKey version' only if the JSON is formatted correctly for that version. There is no evidence of graceful unknown-property handling or of a declared schema version with forward-compat guarantees - the pattern is that a theme is validated against the running build and either loads or does not. Real-world consequence: SwiftKey updates repeatedly broke community themes, and the community theme scene (rwiftkey / Telegram channels) is now marked discontinued. [uncertain - no documentation of unknown-property handling exists; inference from breakage reports and the three-place version-bump requirement]
color_extraction_dynamic_tinting: Predominantly pre-baked. Authored and store themes carry fixed color values in their XML/manifest; there is no evidence SwiftKey consumes Android 12+ Material You / 'monet' wallpaper colors for its keyboard theme the way Gboard's Dynamic Color theme does. The one genuinely dynamic behavior is on the LEGIBILITY axis rather than the palette axis: iOS Photo Themes auto-compute an 'optimum brightness' from the chosen photo, which is image analysis driving a scrim value rather than color extraction driving a palette. Android Photo Themes do not do even that - they apply the fixed 45% default and wait for the user. Notably SwiftKey does NOT recolor key labels from the photo; like Gboard it keeps labels on a fixed light treatment and manages legibility through the scrim plus the key-border/key-background escape hatches. [uncertain - the absence of Material You integration is an inference from the absence of any such documented feature; a recent Android build could have added it without wide coverage]
contrast_enforcement_accessibility: SwiftKey is the closest of the three to actual automated legibility enforcement, but only on iOS and only as a heuristic, not a validated contrast check. There is no evidence of WCAG or APCA ratio computation against the composited background on either platform. What exists: (1) IOS AUTO-BRIGHTNESS - SwiftKey 'will try and determine the optimum brightness for your photo' before the user touches anything, meaning the default state of a new photo theme is already dimmed proportionally to that specific image. This is a genuinely better default than Gboard's 'make the user choose' and better than SwiftKey's own Android behavior. (2) ANDROID FIXED DEFAULT - 45% brightness applied regardless of image content, with the user free to make it worse. (3) ESCAPE HATCHES, and SwiftKey has more of them than Gboard: Android 'key borders' on/off gives each key a bounded surface; Android 'symbols on keys' on/off removes the secondary glyph clutter that is hardest to read over a photo (a legibility control Gboard does not have); iOS 'key background: shades of grey or transparent' is a direct per-key scrim; iOS key pop-up color is separately settable so the pop-up does not inherit an illegible combination. (4) Separately, SwiftKey ships high-contrast built-in themes in its gallery as an authored rather than computed solution. Net assessment: the burden still sits with the user, but SwiftKey gives the user more and better-aimed tools than Gboard does, and iOS at least starts from a content-aware default. [uncertain - no source describes any contrast-ratio validation; the characterization of iOS auto-brightness as a heuristic rather than a validated check is inference]
background_geometry_adaptation: Resolved at creation time by an explicit user crop, then scaled - same strategy as Gboard, with a documented platform asymmetry. The creation flow puts the photo inside a boundary box and lets the user 'pinch to zoom in and out of your photo' and 'drag your photo around within the boundary box to reposition it'. iOS additionally allows ROTATION with the same pinching motion; Microsoft explicitly documents that on Android 'it's not possible to rotate your photo at present'. After that single crop is committed, the same crop must survive every later geometry change: portrait/landscape, SwiftKey's resizable keyboard, one-handed/thumb mode, split mode on tablets and foldables, and the floating/undocked keyboard. There is a documented failure in exactly this area that is worth recording as a cautionary case: Microsoft shipped a fix so that 'Photo Theme previews will now show the correct aspect ratio on newer devices' - i.e. as device aspect ratios changed (taller 19.5:9+ screens), SwiftKey's preview and the real keyboard rect fell out of agreement and previews rendered at the wrong aspect. That is the single most concrete real-world warning available on this topic: a fixed crop plus a preview surface whose aspect is hardcoded or assumed WILL drift as hardware aspect ratios change. Mitigation for a clone: derive the crop boundary box from the live computed keyboard rect for the current device/configuration, never from a constant, and re-derive the preview from the same code path that renders the real keyboard. [uncertain - the exact scale mode applied per configuration (center-crop vs fit) is not documented; the aspect-ratio bug is documented but its root cause is inferred]
layout_locale_independence: The Photo Theme layer is fully layout- and locale-independent by construction - a single image behind the whole keyboard with no per-key registration, so number row on/off, non-QWERTY layouts (SwiftKey supports a very large language/layout set), RTL locales, and split layouts change only the grid drawn on top. The AUTHORED theme layer is partially layout-bound in a specific and instructive way: because slots are addressed by role-plus-state filenames and 9-patches, art stretches correctly across variable key widths (that is exactly what 9-patch solves) and adapts to differing key counts without per-layout variants, but any role a given layout does not instantiate simply goes unused, and any role a layout needs that the theme did not ship falls back to a default. SwiftKey's very wide language support makes this the pragmatic choice. The 'symbols on keys' toggle interacts here: layouts that carry heavy secondary-symbol annotation benefit most from being able to switch those glyphs off over a photo. [uncertain - fallback behavior for missing role assets is inferred from how Android resource resolution and the community's partial-theme workflow behave, not documented]
non_key_surface_coverage: Broad, and the format supports it because non-key chrome is just more role slots in the same resources folder. Covered: the prediction/candidate bar (SwiftKey's signature three-word prediction strip sits on the theme surface and is themed with it), the toolbar/hub row, the emoji and sticker panels, key-press pop-ups (a first-class separately-colorable target on iOS), and the long-press mini-keyboard for accents/alternates. The clipboard panel and in-keyboard settings sheets follow the theme's surface colors. Photo Themes extend the photo across the full keyboard surface including the prediction bar, which is why the brightness scrim has to cover that region too. No evidence that SwiftKey tints the Android system navigation bar the way Gboard does - that appears to be a Gboard-specific touch. [uncertain - per-surface coverage is observational; Microsoft's docs do not enumerate which surfaces a theme covers, and nav-bar behavior is a negative inference from the absence of any coverage of such a feature]
sound_haptic_theming: Not themed - sound and vibration are global preferences decoupled from the visual theme, the same posture as Gboard and unlike Samsung's Keys Cafe. SwiftKey exposes keypress sound on/off and keypress vibration on/off with an intensity control, under its own Typing/Sound & vibration settings rather than under Themes; on Android these ride the standard AudioManager/SoundPool and Vibrator paths and are subject to the device's global sound and vibration settings. No theme carries an audio asset, and there is no sound pack concept in the theme package format - the resources folder holds only images and XML. [uncertain - the specific platform APIs used are inferred from Android norms; the absence of audio in the theme package is a negative inference from every description of the format listing only image assets, style sheets and metadata]
platform_apis_frameworks: Android: InputMethodService, custom Views with Canvas drawing, NinePatchDrawable / StateListDrawable / XML shape drawables, and a runtime resource loader that resolves theme drawables from an unpacked directory in the app's private data rather than only from compiled APK resources (this is the architecturally distinctive piece - it is what makes downloadable themes possible without shipping a new APK). Density-bucket resolution via the standard Android resource ladder. Gallery/photo picker for Photo Theme image selection, and ZIP handling for downloaded theme packages. iOS (documented era): keyboard app extension with UIKit custom views, App Groups shared container for passing themes and settings from the containing app into the extension - which is exactly why Full Access is required. CoreText is used for glyph rendering and is the source of a documented long-running emoji memory-retention issue in the iOS extension. [uncertain - all specific class/API choices are inferred from the observable format and platform norms; Microsoft publishes no architecture documentation]
delivery_installation_pipeline: Three distinct routes, and unlike Gboard, SwiftKey has a real first-party downloadable-theme channel - this is the most relevant reference of the three for anyone building a theme store. (1) OFFICIAL GALLERY - the user opens the SwiftKey app, taps 'Themes', then 'Gallery' to browse designs; themes download over the network as ZIP packages and are written to /sdcard/Android/data/com.touchtype.swiftkey/themes, then unpacked/registered for the keyboard. SwiftKey launched a paid theme store (iOS store launched May 2015) and later made ALL themes free on both platforms, so the current model is a free curated first-party gallery with Microsoft continuously adding designs, not a UGC marketplace - there is no public submission path for third-party theme authors. (2) BUNDLED - built-in themes ship inside the APK at assets/themes. (3) USER-GENERATED PHOTO THEMES - created in-app, stored locally, and critically NOT synced: Microsoft explicitly documents that 'it is not currently possible to use Backup & Sync to save your Photo themes to your Microsoft SwiftKey Account', so photo themes do not transfer between devices or platforms and are lost on uninstall. That is a notable product gap to avoid repeating. (4) COMMUNITY/ROOT (unsupported) - .rwift/.zip packages installed by rwiftkey-themes, which must place files into /data/data/com.touchtype.swiftkey and therefore requires root; the historical alternative was the SwiftkeyXthemes Xposed module, which hooked SwiftKey's theme loading to read themelist.json from external storage so themes could live on /sdcard without repacking the APK on every update. The legacy signed-theme-APK era is dead: SwiftKey verified theme APKs were signed with its own keys, which is why the community moved to file placement and hooking.
permission_store_policy_surface: Android: enabling any IME requires the explicit system keyboard-enable flow plus Android's standard 'may collect all the text you type' warning. Photo selection uses the gallery/photo picker. Downloaded themes are pure data/asset packages, not code, which is what keeps the gallery compatible with Play policy - a theme channel that shipped executable content would not be permissible. Because the gallery is first-party curated rather than UGC, Play's user-generated-content moderation and reporting obligations largely do not bite. iOS: SwiftKey requires FULL ACCESS, and Microsoft's support documentation lists theming as one of the explicit reasons - Full Access is needed because SwiftKey 'stores language models, personalized learning and keyboard preferences outside the keyboard extensions framework' and it enables 'management of settings from the app' and 'further customization with themes'. That is a first-party statement that on iOS, app-to-extension theme sharing is gated behind Full Access, which is the single most important policy fact for any iOS keyboard-theming product: without Full Access there is no shared container, and without a shared container a theme created in your app cannot reach your extension. Apple shows a privacy warning at that grant, which is a real conversion cost. Also relevant: Microsoft discontinued and delisted SwiftKey for iOS on 5 October 2022 (later reversing course after backlash), a reminder that the iOS keyboard business is structurally hard. Downloadable theme content on iOS must remain data-only under App Store rules against downloading executable code. [uncertain - the characterization of Play/App Store policy consequences is analysis rather than quotation of a specific enforcement action against SwiftKey]
memory_performance_budget: Android: no hard per-IME ceiling; the density-bucketed asset model keeps decoded footprint proportional to screen density rather than to the largest shipped asset, which is the main structural mitigation. iOS: the binding constraint and well documented in SwiftKey's own history. Apple's app-extension limit for keyboards is roughly 30-40 MB DIRTY memory with about 77 MB total footprint before the extension is terminated; exceeding it kills the keyboard, and 'excessive memory consumption can eventually cause the keyboard to crash as more content is rendered on the screen'. SwiftKey has concrete public evidence of hitting these walls: a documented CoreText emoji glyph memory-retention problem in the iOS keyboard extension persisting for years, and a shipped fix for 'a crash for iOS users who use the Shooting Stars theme' - i.e. a specific THEME crashing the extension, which is direct evidence that theme assets are a real contributor to the memory budget, not a rounding error. Mitigations implied by the design: Photo Theme images are cropped and downsampled at creation time in the containing app; only one background bitmap is resident; no animated backgrounds exist to hold decoders open; and assets are density-matched so no oversized bitmap is decoded. Practical numbers for a clone targeting the same iOS ceiling: budget under ~10 MB for the entire decoded theme layer, downsample the background to the keyboard rect in points x scale, use a single cached decoded bitmap evicted on theme switch, and never decode a full-resolution camera image inside the extension. [uncertain - the exact iOS limits vary by iOS version and device and Apple does not publish a firm number; the ~30-40 MB dirty / 77 MB total figures come from developer-community measurement]
untrusted_theme_validation_security: SwiftKey is the only one of the three with a real untrusted-content ingestion path (downloaded theme ZIPs), so it necessarily has some handling, but none of it is documented. What is known about the trust model rather than the mechanisms: the legacy theme-APK era used SIGNATURE VERIFICATION as the primary control - SwiftKey checked that a theme APK was signed with its own keys and refused others, which is a strong, simple authenticity control and the reason the community had to use root or Xposed instead. The modern gallery is first-party and served over the network, so authenticity is again controlled at the source rather than by validating arbitrary user-supplied packages. The community .rwift path deliberately bypasses everything by requiring root. No documentation exists on zip-slip / path-traversal protection during theme extraction, decode-bounds limits, entry-count or uncompressed-size caps, or malformed-themelist.json handling - and the fact that a malformed or version-mismatched themelist.json simply causes the theme not to load suggests fail-closed parsing at minimum. For a clone accepting downloaded themes, the transferable control is SwiftKey's: sign the package and verify the signature before extracting anything, then still apply path-traversal and decode-size limits on extraction. [uncertain - all extraction-time hardening is unknown; only the historical APK signature check is attested]
open_source_reference_availability: SwiftKey itself is closed source with no theme SDK and no published schema, but it has the best community reverse-engineering trail of the three. Useful references: github.com/VegaBobo/rwiftkey-themes - the primary source for the .rwift/.zip package structure, the UUID folder + themelist.json layout, the themelist_custom.json rename requirement, and the root/data-dir install path; github.com/nijel8/XSwiftkey (SwiftkeyXthemes on the Xposed repo, bg.nijel.xswiftkey) - an Xposed module that hooks SwiftKey's theme loading to read themes from external storage, and whose 'Method_Hooks_Explaned.txt' documents which SwiftKey methods are intercepted, making it the closest thing to a description of SwiftKey's theme-loading code path; plus the XDA SwiftKey theming threads which document the assets/themes layout, density folders, 9-patch naming, and the APK signature check. Both community projects are effectively discontinued. For an actually studyable theming implementation, an open-source Android keyboard (FlorisBoard, HeliBoard, OpenBoard) remains the better primary reference; SwiftKey's value here is as a documented FORMAT precedent and as the source of the 45% scrim default.
authoring_tooling_preview_generation: First-party authoring is consumer-only - there is no public theme editor, no SDK, and no third-party submission pipeline, so store thumbnails and preview variants are produced internally by Microsoft's own design process and nothing about their requirements is public. The in-app Photo Theme flow does provide LIVE PREVIEW: the user sees the keyboard rendered with the photo while adjusting crop and brightness, and on iOS the key pop-up color picker explicitly lets you 'preview choices using the keyboard view'. The documented aspect-ratio preview bug (previews showing the wrong aspect on newer devices until fixed) is a direct warning that the preview surface and the real keyboard must share a code path. Community authoring tooling exists but is crude and format-level rather than visual: the historical XDA workflow is to unpack a theme, hand-edit PNG/9-patch and XML files across density folders, bump version numbers in all three required places, repack, and install via root or Xposed - no WYSIWYG editor was ever built for SwiftKey the way Rboard Theme Creator was for Gboard.
cross_platform_token_parity: Explicitly NO parity, and Microsoft says so directly - 'all themes are unique across platforms, and cannot be transferred from Microsoft SwiftKey Keyboard for Android to iOS (or vice versa) at this time'. This is a first-party statement, which makes SwiftKey the clearest documented case that a single theme definition rendering on both platforms is not what the market leaders actually do. The Photo Theme controls themselves diverge feature-by-feature: rotation is iOS-only, key borders and symbols-on-keys toggles are Android-only, key pop-up color and key background (grey/transparent) are iOS-only, and auto-computed brightness is iOS-only versus Android's fixed 45% default. On top of that, Photo Themes do not even sync BETWEEN devices on the same platform, since Backup & Sync does not cover them. Inherently platform-bound properties: anything depending on the iOS App Group shared container, the Android density-bucketed resource ladder, and each platform's native drawable/state model. Design implication: if cross-platform parity matters for your product, that is a differentiator versus SwiftKey rather than a pattern to copy from it - and the way to get it is to define themes as a platform-neutral token document (colors, scrim alpha, crop rect, flags) with per-platform renderers, rather than as a bag of platform-native drawables the way SwiftKey does.
animation_budget: OPEN / WEAKLY DOCUMENTED, though less open than for Gboard because there is one concrete data point. SwiftKey Photo Themes are strictly static rasters - no Lottie, GIF, or video backgrounds, and no documented frame-rate cap or idle-pause policy because there is no ambient animation to govern. The one hint that SwiftKey's authored themes carry more than static art is the 'Shooting Stars' theme, which by name implies a motion or particle effect and which Microsoft shipped a crash fix for on iOS - suggesting that where SwiftKey does animate, it is a built-in first-party theme with bespoke code rather than a data-driven animation format any theme can declare, and that it was expensive enough to crash a memory-constrained extension. Interaction-level motion (key press feedback, pop-ups, flow/swipe trail) exists on both platforms and is not theme-authorable. Verdict: no user-authorable animation of any kind; the sole animated-theme evidence is a first-party theme that caused a documented iOS crash. That crash is itself the strongest available argument for treating animated keyboard backgrounds as a high-risk feature on iOS. [uncertain - 'Shooting Stars' being genuinely animated is inferred from its name plus the crash report; its actual implementation is not documented]
